core_concepts: Foundations
Structured thinking starts with the claim that complex topics become easier to understand when the author separates observation , interpretation , and decision
The chapter defines a working model
Why the distinction matters
The distinction matters because the same evidence can support several plausible interpretations
The chapter also introduces a qualifier
Observation refers to what can be directly described
Interpretation refers to the meaning assigned to those descriptions
Decision refers to the action chosen after weighing competing interpretations

Method The method chapter turns the framework into a repeatable process

It argues that good summaries and decisions emerge from a short sequence of moves: collect the main claims, identify the causal logic, test the limits of each claim, and only then compress the material
The reader asks how the concepts connect, which claims are foundational, and which claims merely illustrate the larger pattern
This process works because compression after analysis is safer than compression before analysis
If the writer shortens too early, they often keep vivid phrases while dropping the mechanism that made the phrase meaningful
It should preserve technical terms when they carry meaning, yet it should gloss them once if a new reader may not know them
A structured process can reduce confusion, but it cannot remove disagreement when people have different values, incentives, or risk tolerances
The method is most reliable when the subject has enough stability for concepts to transfer across cases
It is less reliable when the environment changes quickly, because the relationships that explained yesterday's result may not explain tomorrow's
